title: A leak in a tidy pipeline
promptMarkdown:
*The scenario and all numbers are synthetic; no real organisation or dataset is described.*

At the start of record week t, a team wants to predict whether a machine will fail during the following week t+1. The allowed sensor features summarise information available before that start-of-week cutoff. There are 5,000 records from 250 machines, with 20 consecutive record weeks per machine and eventual outcome label `fails_next_week`; the observed base rate is 6%. Their pipeline is:

1. Fit imputation and standardisation on all 5,000 records.
2. Add `ticket_opened_this_week`, an indicator filled retrospectively after observing the entire record week t. Tickets follow fault detection, sometimes in the failure week and sometimes the preceding week. No sensitivity, specificity or joint counts are supplied.
3. Shuffle records and split them 80/20 into training and a named test set, without respecting machine identity or chronology.
4. Train a two-layer MLP.
5. Try 30 hyperparameter configurations and select the highest named-test accuracy.
6. Report 97.4% accuracy as evidence for future failure prediction on new machines.

(a) Identify the demonstrated information-boundary violations and plausible leakage risks. Use the unit taxonomy, but do not claim that literal duplicate rows or direct neighbouring-label access were established without evidence.
(b) Compute the majority baseline. Explain what 97.4% does and does not show, including the need for per-class outcomes and an independent evaluation. Which inflation effects cannot be quantified from the supplied aggregates?
(c) Give a conditional assessment of the most serious risks. State the extra measurements needed to compare their sizes; no unique numeric ranking is implied by this scenario.
(d) Give a corrected protocol in at most ten lines: independent machines and appropriate time periods, prediction-time feature eligibility, training-only transforms, validation selection, outcome-availability gaps, frozen final evaluation, seeds, baselines and uncertainty. Then state its ten-point information contract: observed inputs; target; history in training; history at inference; person/entity; task; later time periods; unavailable information; simplest baseline; claims not tested.
hintLadder: For each feature, ask: at the moment the prediction would be used (the start of the week), is this value known yet? If not, how did it get into the training data?

A neighbouring record has a different prediction week. Which actual features or label access would reveal the target outcome, and which such access has the prompt established? Separate possible temporal dependence from proven direct label leakage.

An 80/20 row split can place many weeks from the same machine on both sides. What machine-specific information could carry across, and how does that differ from evaluation on entirely new machines? Do not assume all nineteen other weeks are in training.
Step 5 picks the maximum of 30 test accuracies. What is the expected maximum of 30 noisy, roughly unbiased estimates compared with any one of them?
The baseline is the accuracy of a model that never predicts a failure. Compute it from the base rate.

deterministicChecks.description: the majority baseline of 94% is computed
asserting that the pipeline is sound or leak-free, or that 97.4% demonstrates predictive skill

criteria.criterion: Identifies the retrospective ticket flag as unavailable at the specified start-of-week cutoff; does not assert a near-copy of the label or its standalone accuracy without joint data.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Named without the mechanism or misclassified.

criteria.criterion: Explains group/time mismatch for new-machine future prediction, test-based selection and full-data preprocessing; distinguishes possible dependence from demonstrated literal duplicates or direct label access.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Group, temporal and selection leaks all identified; preprocessing leak noted.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Two of the three major leaks identified.

criteria.criterion: Computes the 94% majority baseline, limits the interpretation of the selected 97.4%, requests per-class evidence and recognises that leak inflation cannot be quantified or uniquely ranked from these aggregates.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Baseline computed, at least two leaks' effects discussed, selection bias on the test set explained.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Baseline computed but the inflation argument is thin.

criteria.criterion: Defines machine/time-aware partitions with outcome-availability gaps, eligible features, training-only transforms, validation selection, frozen independent final evaluation and a complete information contract.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Most elements present; one major gap (e.g. still tunes on test).

checkExamples.label: complete audit
checkExamples.text: The retrospective ticket feature is unavailable at the prediction cutoff. Its exact relation to next-week failure is unknown, so its predictive accuracy cannot be inferred. Fitting transforms on all records violates the training boundary. Random row splitting allows machine and time overlap, which may exploit dependence and does not test future prediction on new machines; literal duplicates and direct neighbouring-label access are not established. Choosing among 30 configurations by test accuracy contaminates that test for selection. The majority baseline is 94%. The selected 97.4% requires independent, machine/time-aware evaluation and per-class outcomes; the size of each inflation effect is unknown.

checkExamples.label: denial of the problem
checkExamples.text: There is no leak in this pipeline; the pipeline is sound and 97.4% shows strong predictive skill.

checkExamples.label: baseline written as a proportion
checkExamples.text: A model that never predicts a failure has accuracy 0.94 on this data, so the reported figure must be judged against that.
